page.title: Flavor Improver | Simon Cui
hero.title: Improving dairy flavor with Bayesian optimization
hero.intro: Developing the flavor of a product means adjusting the recipe again and again, and every round needs a sensory evaluation, which is slow and expensive. Bayesian optimization is a search method that learns from every trial and tries to reach the target with as few trials as possible. This page demonstrates the idea with a virtual evaluation function in place of a sensory panel: pick a dairy product as the base, set a direction of improvement, and watch the algorithm decide which flavor compounds to add and how much.
hero.disclaimer: This is a demonstration of a method, not a recipe recommendation. The evaluation function is built from single-molecule odor predictions and a simplified additive rule, and it ignores masking, synergy and matrix effects. In real work it would be replaced by a sensory panel or GC-O experiments; the value of Bayesian optimization is reaching the target with as few trials as possible.

method.title: How it works
flow.1.title: Set a direction
flow.1.sub: which odors to strengthen or weaken
flow.2.title: Try a recipe
flow.3.title: Evaluate
flow.4.title: Update the model
flow.4.sub: a Gaussian process learns recipe → score
flow.5.title: Pick the next recipe
flow.5.sub: the acquisition function balances exploring and exploiting
flow.loop: Steps 2 to 5 repeat until the trial budget is used up
method.gp: A Gaussian process is a surrogate model: from the trials done so far it estimates how well any new recipe would score, and how uncertain that estimate is. The further a recipe is from anything already tried, the larger the uncertainty.
method.acq: The acquisition function decides what to try next. Think of looking for the highest point in hilly country you cannot see: search near the high places you already know (exploitation), but also try places you have never been (exploration). This project uses Expected Improvement: choose the recipe expected to beat the best result so far by the largest margin.
formula.1: Odor activity value: OAV<sub>i</sub> = concentration<sub>i</sub> ÷ threshold<sub>i</sub>
formula.2: Perceived intensity: I<sub>i</sub> = log<sub>10</sub>(OAV<sub>i</sub>), and I<sub>i</sub> = 0 when OAV<sub>i</sub> ≤ 1
formula.3: Odor profile = normalize(Σ I<sub>i</sub> × v<sub>i</sub>), where v<sub>i</sub> is the descriptor vector of compound i
formula.5: Score = cosine(improved, target) − 0.05 × max(0, number added − 5) − 0.002 × log<sub>10</sub>(1 + Σ added OAV)
method.params: What the terms mean. Cosine similarity measures how close the shapes of two profiles are; 1 means identical. The last two terms are penalties: each additive beyond 5 costs 0.05, and larger total additions cost more. In other words, simpler recipes with smaller additions are more practical. Each candidate is searched between 0.01 and 100 times its threshold.
method.lift: Descriptor vectors. The odor of each compound comes from the odor prediction model of project 1: it predicts the probability of 12 dairy-related descriptors, which is then divided by how often that descriptor occurs in the training data (the "lift"). Without this correction, common descriptors such as sweet and fruity have high probabilities for almost everything and would dominate every profile.
method.no_decrease: Important property: in this additive model, adding compounds cannot directly lower the intensity of an odor. "Less sour" can only be reached by strengthening other odors so that sourness takes a smaller share. Real foods also show masking, which this model does not include.
results.title: Does Bayesian optimization help?
results.intro: Each example was run with 4 methods, 10 times each (10 random seeds), 100 trials per run. The table shows the best score found in each run (mean ± standard deviation); the number in brackets is the average number of additives in the best recipe.
results.m.bo_sparse_init: Bayesian optimization (10 sparse random starting recipes)
results.m.bo: Bayesian optimization (10 uniform random starting recipes)
results.m.random_sparse: Random search (1 to 5 random compounds per trial)
results.m.random_uniform: Random search (random amounts of all 18 compounds)
results.table_note: Bold marks the method with the highest mean score for each example. Uniform random search scores low because it almost always adds many compounds and is penalized for it.
results.takeaway: Conclusion: both Bayesian optimization variants beat random search consistently in most examples (Mann-Whitney test p < 0.05 in most comparisons), but the gains are small. The main reason is that the base is already close to the target (the target is a small adjustment of the base), so there is little room to improve. Also, 44% to 97% of the additions in Bayesian optimization recipes sit at the upper limit of 100 times the threshold: in an additive model, adding more of a compound only strengthens its odor and has no downside, so the algorithm tends to push to the limit.
known.title: Known-answer test
known.intro: Method: add 1 to 3 random candidate compounds to the base (10 to 100 times their threshold), use the resulting profile as the target, and check whether the optimizer finds those compounds again. Each case was run 3 times.
known.note: Results for Bayesian optimization with uniform random starting recipes. Compound overlap = intersection ÷ union of the found and the true compounds.
known.takeaway: Conclusion: the profile is almost always recovered (similarity 0.997 or higher), but the compounds themselves are often only partly recovered. Many compounds have very similar descriptor vectors (for example several lactones, or several diketones), so different combinations give nearly the same profile. In other words, an odor profile alone does not determine a unique recipe. The test could not be run for the two Gouda cheeses: they already contain many compounds with high OAVs, so adding 1 to 3 candidates (at most 100 times the threshold) changes the profile too little (cosine similarity stays above 0.98) to make a meaningful target.
jsbo.title: The optimizer in your browser
jsbo.text: After you change thresholds, a simplified Bayesian optimization runs in plain JavaScript (Gaussian process with an isotropic RBF kernel, Expected Improvement maximized over random candidate recipes, 60 trials). With the default thresholds and compared with a random search of the same 60 trials (10 random seeds per example), it scored higher in {wins} of 40 runs, again by a small margin. Its evaluation function was checked against the Python version and agrees to within 10<sup>−9</sup>.
history.title: Parameter changes during development
history.1: The penalty on the total amount added was first set to 0.01. Adding nothing then scored best, because the penalty was larger than the achievable gain in similarity. After review it was changed to 0.002 and every method was re-run.
history.2: The upper limit of each addition was first 1000 times the threshold, and many recipes pushed several compounds to that limit, which is unrealistic. It was lowered to 100 times and everything was re-run. The run played on this page (random seed 0) was fixed before the experiments; results were not cherry-picked.
limits.title: Limitations
limits.1: The evaluation function is virtual. It ignores masking, synergy and matrix effects of real mixtures. Suggested recipes must be tested experimentally and cannot be used in products directly.
limits.2: The additive model cannot directly lower an odor; it can only change the relative shares of odors.
limits.3: Single-molecule odors are predictions of the project 1 model and contain errors.
limits.4: Thresholds are literature values in water, and base concentrations come from a single sample in a single study. Values for different media and methods differ by orders of magnitude (see the literature ranges in the table), which is why this page lets you change the thresholds.
limits.5: Gouda concentrations are on a dry-matter basis and the paper does not give the water content needed to convert them, so their OAVs against water thresholds are approximate.
limits.6: Many candidates have very similar odor vectors. The same target can be reached with different recipes, so the specific compounds suggested are not unique.
limits.7: Perceived intensity is approximated by log<sub>10</sub>(OAV); compound-specific concentration-intensity curves are not considered.
limits.8: Cost, regulatory limits, solubility and stability are not considered.
limits.future: Possible next steps: precursor recommendations (from reaction-pathway knowledge); a better mixture model (one attempt is recorded below); cost and regulatory constraints; letting users score the suggestions instead of the virtual evaluation function (human in the loop).
footer.p1: Single-molecule odor prediction: the graph neural network from project 1: Odor Predictor on this site.
footer.thr: Odor thresholds (water): L.J. van Gemert, Odour Thresholds: Compilations of Odour Threshold Values in Air, Water and Other Media, 2nd ed., Oliemans Punter & Partners, 2011. Selected by a rule fixed in advance: the detection threshold of Czerny et al., Eur. Food Res. Technol. 228, 265-273 (2008) first, then the detection threshold of Buttery et al. as compiled there, then Karagül-Yüceer et al. (2003/2004); compounds with none of these were excluded. Acetoin uses 0.8 mg/kg (Buttery et al.).
ref.option: Flavor gap analysis: infant formula vs human milk
ref.notice.1: Under GB 2760-2024 Table B.1, flavorings may not be added to infant formula foods (food category 13.01); its footnote states that no flavoring at all may be added to formula whose range covers infants aged 0 to 6 months. This example concerns infant formula, so it does not recommend adding flavor compounds and only points to precursor directions.
ref.notice.2: Any use of precursors must comply with the product standards for infant formula (such as GB 10765-2021) and the standard for nutrient fortifiers (GB 14880).
ref.notice.3: Raising precursors such as unsaturated fatty acids may increase the risk of oxidized off-flavors; this has to be assessed together with processing and storage conditions.
ref.notice.4: This page only compares the odor profiles of two published data sets to illustrate an analysis method. It is not an evaluation of, or a claim about, any product.
ref.input_intro: Both data sets can be edited: choose a starting sample, change concentrations, or add and remove compounds. Compounds with a bold OAV meet the key-odorant criterion and are used in the analysis below; the others are not. Thresholds follow the fixed rule of examples 1 to 4 (detection thresholds in water, van Gemert 2011); in this example, compounds for which Buttery et al. give only a narrow range (ends differing by at most 2 times) use its geometric mean.
ref.side_hm_desc: Fresh mature milk (infants aged 2 to 17 months), foremilk and hindmilk combined, kept at 0 to 4 °C and analyzed within 1 h, not frozen. Mothers differ a lot; you can replace the values with your own means or measurements.
ref.side_if_desc: Stage 1 (0 to 6 months) cow-milk-based formula powders of 6 brands, analyzed right after opening. Brand names are not shown.
ref.side_note_hm: Concentrations from Table 2 of the paper.
ref.side_note_if: Concentration = value in Table 3 of the paper (per kg powder) ÷ 8, converted to reconstituted formula with the ratio used in the paper (about 4.3 g powder in 30 mL water).
ref.radar_cap: Calculated from the key odorants only, with the same rule as examples 1 to 4. Each axis is an odor descriptor; values are shares (they sum to 1). Descriptor vectors use the lift, which inflates rare descriptors such as fishy, mushroom and metallic.
ref.gap_title: Key odorants with the largest gaps
ref.no_gap: No key odorant in the current input has data on both sides.
ref.gap_def: Gap = |log₁₀ OAV(formula) − log₁₀ OAV(human milk)|, only for compounds with data on both sides and OAV ≥ {cutoff} on at least one side.
ref.only_hm: Data for human milk only (no concentration on the formula side, no gap calculated): {list}.
ref.only_if: Data for formula only (no concentration on the human milk side, no gap calculated): {list}.
ref.cos: Cosine similarity of the two profiles: {cos} (1 means identical shapes).
ref.dir.if_higher: {compound}: higher in formula. Its precursor is {precursor}; the gap mainly reflects oxidation of the precursor during processing and storage, so the direction is to control oxidation (heating, oxygen, storage conditions), not to add precursor.
ref.dir.hm_higher: {compound}: higher in human milk. The related precursor is {precursor}; any adjustment has to stay within the ranges of GB 10765-2021, and the risk of oxidized off-flavors has to be assessed.
ref.dir.none: {compound}: no precursor information in the table yet.
ref.no_amount: This analysis gives no addition amounts. How much of a precursor turns into an odorant depends on processing and storage conditions, which the model cannot predict quantitatively. About the data: both data sets come from the same study and method (headspace SPME, external standard calibration) and are semi-quantitative; odorants in human milk vary a lot between mothers and with the maternal diet.
ref.lower_intro: Bold compounds are key odorants in the current input. Every row gives the source and where in it the statement is found; the regulatory status refers to the use of the precursor in infant formula.
ref.pcol.status: Use in infant formula and regulatory basis
ref.reg_official: The official text of the standards prevails.
ref.sim_title: Addition simulation (method demonstration only, not applicable to infant formula)
ref.sim_warning: Method demonstration only. Under GB 2760-2024 no flavoring may be added to infant formula, so the result below cannot be used for infant formula. It only shows what the optimizer of examples 1 to 4 would suggest when starting from the key odorants of the formula and using the human milk profile as the reference. The additive model cannot lower existing odorants, so compounds that are higher in formula cannot be offset by additions.
ref.sim_note: Only additions of at least 1 times the threshold are listed. Results differ between runs because of randomness.
footer.ref5: Flavor gap analysis, infant formula vs human milk: concentrations from Zhang et al., Food Chem 382, 132348 (2022); sources for the precursor table are given in each row.
mix.title: Tried: a mixture odor similarity model (not adopted)
mix.why: Why: the additive rule on this page sums the odor profiles of the compounds by intensity and ignores masking and synergy in real mixtures, the largest limitation of this project. In 2026, work by the Monell Chemical Senses Center, Yale University, IBM Research and others showed that odor-descriptor features of single molecules predict fairly well how similar two mixtures smell (Satarifard et al., PNAS 2026). Following this idea, we tried to train a small model that compares two mixtures, meant only for the reference-food example (where the target is itself a real mixture), not for the directional targets of examples 1-4.
mix.how: How: the large dataset of that study has no open licence (the challenge terms forbid other uses), so only the public human similarity ratings of Snitz et al. (2013, CC BY 4.0) were used: pairwise comparisons of intensity-matched molecules or mixtures, rated 0-100. A mixture is the power mean of its components' predicted odor vectors (138 descriptors) and the distance is an angle with learned per-descriptor weights. The split is by mixture: experiments 2 and 3 (165 pairs) for training and cross-validation, the 141 non-overlapping pairs of experiment 1 as the test set, computed once. The table shows the correlation between predicted distance and human ratings (dissimilarity) on the test set.
mix.row.b12: Baseline: this page's additive rule (cosine of 12-dimension profiles)
mix.row.b138: Baseline: additive rule with the 138 predicted probabilities
mix.result: Result: the new model has the highest Pearson correlation but a lower Spearman correlation than the Snitz angle and the 138-dimension additive rule, and every 95% confidence interval of its Pearson difference to a baseline includes 0 (resampling mixtures; vs the 21-descriptor Snitz angle [-0.23, +0.24], vs this page's additive rule [-0.02, +0.41]). The replacement criterion fixed in advance (better on both metrics, with a clear difference) was not met, so this page's evaluation function was not changed. One more observation: the 12-dimension additive rule used here is the weakest of all methods, but this was noticed only after seeing the test results, so nothing was changed because of it.
mix.note: The test has limits of its own: training and test data are intensity-matched mixtures outside a food matrix, only about 300 pairs from one laboratory; using it for dairy flavor would also need concentration weights for the components (e.g. by OAV), which these data do not validate. The model predicts overall similarity and cannot tell which masking or synergy is involved.
footer.mix: Mixture similarity experiment (not adopted): data from Snitz K, Yablonka A, Weiss T, Frumin I, Khan RM, Sobel N. Predicting odor perceptual similarity from odor structure. PLoS Comput Biol 2013, 9(9): e1003184. doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003184 (CC BY 4.0); idea from Satarifard V, Sisson L, Han Y, et al. A semantic-based community model for high-fidelity tuning of olfactory mixture distances. PNAS 2026, 123(32): e2611057123. doi:10.1073/pnas.2611057123. Code in training/mixture/.
user.option: My own GC-MS data (sample vs target)
user.intro: Your own data: process the sample (e.g. your formula) and the target (e.g. human milk) one after the other in the GC-MS flavor interpreter and click "Send as the sample" or "Send as the target" in its flavor step; or upload the ranking CSV exported there below. The two can come from different standard files: this page merges them by compound.
user.privacy: Your data are processed and kept in your browser only and are not uploaded. Only when you click "Look up structures on PubChem" below does the page send the CAS numbers or names of the compounds without a structure to PubChem (no amounts or other data).

user.csv_header: This CSV is not recognized: it needs a compound name column (Compound / 化合物 / 物质 / 名称) and at least one value column (amount, relative content or peak area, OAV, ROAV); see "CSV file requirements" above.
user.csv_empty: The file has no compound with a value.
user.storage_off: Local storage is unavailable in this browser; the data are kept only until the page is closed.
user.radar_note: Same profile rule as the examples on this page: each compound's intensity = log₁₀({score}) (when above 1), times its "lift" on each dimension, summed and normalized (dimensions sum to 1). {n} compounds take part (with an odor vector and a threshold, {score} > 1 on at least one side).
user.radar_note_all: Uses the predicted probabilities of all 138 descriptors (no lift); the chart shows the 10 largest descriptors of the two profiles. {n} compounds take part.
user.cos: Cosine similarity of the two profiles: {cos} (1 = identical shape).
user.cos_none: At least one side has no compound for a profile, so no similarity can be computed.
user.no_gaps: No compound has data on both sides and a contribution on at least one.
user.gap_def_oav: Difference = target OAV / sample OAV; an OAV below 1 (not perceptible) or not detected counts as 1; a {fold}-fold difference or more marks one side as higher. Only compounds with data on both sides, a threshold, and OAV > 1 on at least one side are listed.
user.gap_def_roav: Each side is converted to ROAV, then each compound's share of its side's total contribution is compared (share = its log₁₀ ROAV / the sum over all compounds); a difference of {pp} percentage points or more marks one side as higher. ROAV only reflects contributions within a sample, so the ROAV values of the two sides cannot be compared directly.
user.unknown_s: Not in the sample's data, amount unknown (no difference computed): {list}.
user.unknown_t: Not in the target's data, amount unknown (no difference computed): {list}.
user.list_s_intro: The additive rule can only add, not lower existing compounds: these need to be lowered through raw materials or processing (e.g. oxidation control, heat treatment, storage).
user.list_t_intro: These compounds are higher in the target; those with an odor vector appear under "What to add" below.
user.li_t_novec: {name}: {gap} (no odor vector or threshold, not usable as a candidate yet)
user.rules_now: Current rule: one side is higher from a {fold}-fold OAV difference, or a {pp} percentage-point difference in contribution share.

user.rec_notice2: Infant formula: under GB 2760-2024, flavorings may not be added to infant formula, so such products can only be adjusted through raw materials, processing and precursors; see also the precursor table of example 5.
user.rec_intro_oav: Ranked by the similarity of the two profiles after raising the compound's intensity in the sample to the target's level; this calculation is only used for ranking, and no amounts are given.

user.rec_unmeasured: Contributing in the target but not in the sample's data: {list}. Check their amounts in the sample first.

hero.own_data: Analyzing your own samples? Choose the last item, "My own GC-MS data", in the example list below (or open this link): process the sample and the target in the GC-MS flavor interpreter first, then compare their OAV or ROAV and odor profiles here and get the compounds to add (directions only, no amounts). Your data are processed in your browser only.
method.user.1: Reading: the GC-MS flavor interpreter matches the targets of your standard file; OAV is computed when amounts are quantified, ROAV when only peak areas are known. The two results (sample, target) are sent to this page or uploaded as CSV and merged by compound.
method.user.2: Profiles: the same additive rule as the examples: intensity = log10(OAV or ROAV), times each compound's odor vector, summed and normalized. Odor vectors are model predictions from the flavor knowledge base; for compounds outside it, this site's model can predict them in your browser from a structure.
method.user.3: Comparison: the cosine similarity of the two profiles; per compound, the OAV ratio (both sides quantified) or the contribution share (at least one side with peak areas only), with an adjustable rule for "higher on one side".
method.user.4: Suggestions: compounds higher in the target are the directions for addition; when both sides are quantified they are ranked by the profile similarity after topping up that one compound to the target's level. Compounds higher in the sample cannot be fixed by adding and are listed separately. No amounts are computed.
limits.9: With your own data: the results depend on how comparable the two data sets are (same sample preparation and instrument method, same quantification); ROAV only reflects contributions within a sample; thresholds are mostly literature values in water, unlike a dairy matrix; model-predicted odor vectors may have larger errors. The suggestions are directions only and must be checked by sensory evaluation.
user.req.1: One sample per file (one file for the sample, one for the target). The first row holds the column names; comma or semicolon separated; UTF-8 encoding (in Excel: Save as → CSV UTF-8). Column names are case-insensitive, in English or Chinese.
user.req.2: Required: a compound name column, named Compound, 化合物, 物质 or 名称.
user.req.3: Required, at least one of these value columns (used in this order when there are several): ① quantified amount (Amount, 浓度 or 含量; unit in the column name, e.g. "Amount (µg/kg)", µg/kg when none) → compared by OAV; ② relative content or peak area (Relative content, 相对含量 or 峰面积) → compared by ROAV; ③ a ready-made OAV (column OAV); ④ a ready-made ROAV (column ROAV).
user.req.4: Recommended: a CAS column (CAS), to match compounds and odors in the flavor knowledge base reliably; an odor threshold column (Odor threshold or 阈值; unit in the column name, mg/kg when none), needed with ① or ②: compounds without one use the built-in value, and those without a built-in value are left out; no threshold is needed when OAV or ROAV is given.
user.req.5: Compounds that were not detected can be written as "not detected" or "未检出" in the value column. The file from "Export the ranking (CSV)" of the GC-MS flavor interpreter already meets these requirements and can be uploaded as it is.
